card.stem: The sketch shows the external wall and window of a dwelling house. The wall is a 400 mm concrete block wall with full-fill insulated cavity and is plastered on both sides. The fixed frame of the window is 120 mm × 80 mm and is thermally broken.
card.questionText: To a scale of 1:5, draw a vertical section through the external wall and top portion of the window. Show the wall, the concrete lintels, and the top fixed frame of the window. On your drawing, show the typical construction details from a level 400 mm below to a level 400 mm above the concrete lintels. Include three typical dimensions on your drawing.

rows.contextNote: Any 7 x 5 marks. Credit the best SEVEN acceptable details at 5 marks each, capped at 35. Marked details: external render; concrete block outer leaf; full-fill insulated cavity with wall tie; concrete block inner leaf; internal plaster; cavity closer; stepped DPC; concrete lintels; thermally broken window frame; triple glazing; airtightness. The model specifies 19 mm render, 100 mm leaves, a 200 mm insulated cavity, 100 mm × 75 mm concrete lintels, 15 mm plaster and airtightness tape.

options: Full fill insulated cavity with wall tie

rows.contextNote: Three appropriate typical dimensions on the section.
Draughting, accuracy and scale of the section: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4.

card.stem: The sketch shows a living area with a sloped ceiling under construction. The homeowners wish to have a high level of insulation in the sloped ceiling.
card.questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, show one suitable method of highly insulating the sloped ceiling. Show on your sketch how the ceiling is to be finished internally. Specify the type and thickness of insulation.

rows.verbatim: Method of insulating the sloped ceiling note & sketch (8 + 8 marks)
rows.contextNote: Note 8 and sketch 8 of one method, showing the internal finish. Such as: insulation cut to fit between the rafters with a ventilation space below the breather membrane, an airtight membrane over the insulated rafters, then plasterboard or insulated plasterboard fixed to the rafters and skimmed or taped and filled; or a ventilation card between the rafters with spray-foam insulation trimmed flush, then plasterboard and skim.

rows.verbatim: Preferred insulation type for sloped ceiling
rows.contextNote: Such as: expanded polystyrene (EPS), phenolic, polyisocyanurate (PIR) or extruded polystyrene (XPS); the method notes also name wood fibre and sheep’s wool.
At least 200 mm of insulation.

card.stem: The image shows a portion of a site location map. A and B are two sites being considered for a new dwelling house in the countryside.
card.questionText: Select your preferred site A or B, and give two reasons for your choice.

rows.contextNote: Select site A or site B.

One reason for the chosen site. Such as, for site A: a south-facing façade for solar gain; direct access to the main road for services; close to existing houses; hedgerow shelter; a well-proportioned site.
A second, different reason. Such as, for site B: safer access from a secondary road; off the main road for privacy, with less noise and air pollution; close to existing houses and services.

card.questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: raft foundation; housing joint; rainwater butt; stud wall; laser level; damp-proof course; door threshold; baluster; room thermostat.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Raft foundation: a large, continuous reinforced concrete slab supporting the whole structure, "floating" like a raft; spreads the load over the whole footprint, reducing pressure on the soil; suits soils of low bearing capacity; needs more steel and concrete than a strip foundation. Housing joint: a groove or slot cut across the width of one piece receives the end of another; a medium gluing area; used for shelves, cabinets and bookcases; a through housing runs fully across and shows at both ends, a stopped housing hides the joint at the front edge. Rainwater butt: a container that collects and stores rainwater from the roof via gutters and downpipes; reuses water for plants, lawns or washing the car; reduces reliance on treated tap water and lowers metered water use. Stud wall: an internal wall framed with vertical timber or metal studs covered with plasterboard on both sides; lighter and faster to build than a block wall; load-bearing or non-load-bearing; houses electrical and plumbing services; poorer sound insulation and bearing capacity than a block wall. Laser level: a tool projecting a laser beam to give a straight, level reference line, vertical and/or horizontal; a rotary laser projects a 360° beam for large or outdoor work; more accurate than a spirit level; can be mounted on tripods or clamps. Damp-proof course: a barrier stopping moisture rising through walls and floors by capillary action; polythene, bitumen felt, lead or copper, or slate; laid horizontally between courses, typically 150 mm above ground level, and around window and door openings; protects finishes and reduces mould and decay. Door threshold: the strip of wood, metal or plastic at the bottom of a doorway where the door closes; bridges two floor surfaces and seals the doorway; external thresholds keep out weather and draughts; internal ones cover changes in floor level; must meet building regulations so they are not a trip hazard. Baluster: a short vertical post, often decorative, supporting the handrail of a stairs; a row of balusters is a balustrade; a safety element preventing falls, especially by children; also on balconies and terraces; wood, metal, glass or concrete. Room thermostat: controls room temperature by switching the heating on below the set point and off above it; keeps rooms comfortable efficiently; manual dial or digital models; smart thermostats connect to Wi-Fi and a smartphone.
